Has capitalism had its day? - Journalist Paul Mason at Kings Place London, U.K. (7-22-2015) 1 Hr. 38 Min.

Description:

In the wake of the financial crisis and with the rapid rise of new technologies, award-winning economist and journalist, Paul Mason, believes we are on the cusp of a seismic economic shift, of a kind yet to be seen in human history.

Join Paul as he takes on a panel of renowned journalists and thinkers including Douglas Murray, associate director of the Henry Jackson Society and Spectator columnist, Zoe Williams, Guardian columnist, Julia Powles, a lawyer working on technology law and policy at the University of Cambridge and the Guardian, and Pat Kane, writer, musician, activist & director of The Play Ethic.

In his new book, Post-capitalism: A Guide to Our Future, Paul offers a powerful critique of why capitalism has failed us. A rallying cry to the Left, he argues this is a golden opportunity to shape a new, more socially just and sustainable economy with the emerging forces of information technology, rapid scientific advancement and free, easily-shared goods.

But has capitalism really had its day? The king of all economic systems has thrived for more than five hundred years, seeing off major competition from communism and socialism, time and again proving its resilience in the face of major economic and social crises, emerging transformed, reinvigorated and more powerful than ever. As the country embarks on another five years of Conservative rule, take part in what will be a lively debate on the future of the free market.

Source: Guardian Live | Has capitalism had its day?

Mammoths Died Out Because of Sudden Climate Change

I like to think that's why they went extinct but my cynical side tells me that we as human beings caused their extinction from hunting them. We've been pretty good at wiping species of animals off the face of this earth throughout our existence.

A lot of animals can get set in their ways if left alone too long, so the first disruption that comes along can have completely outsized effects(eg, the dodo was driven to extinction simply because it was incapable of understanding the concept of a predator). If a second disruption follows that, even if neither alone could have a severe impact on the population, the species could be wiped out before it could regroup and evolve behaviors to deal with the new environment.

Isn't that the case for almost every creature in the history of Earth? The status quo that has held the naturally balancing system of eat/eaten gets disrupted by some sort of outside influence that changes the environment in such a way that animals can't adapt fast enough and die out. I mean sure sometimes the climate change isn't that sudden like geological shift or salination/desalination/oxidation/deoxydation but you still end up where a bunch of animals dying because they can't adapt fast enough and die out.

Also is this noteworthy? Nobody writes a news article about how colder south pacific seas are causing a few jellyfish to die out and that's happening as we speak.
